## Buying Your First Car: Should You Buy New, Buy Used or Lease?


---


**Key takeaways:**


- Buying used, buying new and leasing each come with different upfront costs and long-term expenses.
- A lower price or[monthly payment](https://financialwellnesscenter.northwest.bank/credit-and-debt/credit/tools/calculate-a-vehicle-payment?article_source=news_insights&article_category=education&article_name=buying-vs-leasing-your-first-car&article_cta=vehicle-payment-calculator) doesn’t always mean a car will cost less overall, so consider factors such as depreciation, maintenance, insurance and fees.
- Used cars often cost less but may require more upkeep. New cars average may offer greater reliability at a higher price, while leasing can mean lower[monthly payments](https://financialwellnesscenter.northwest.bank/credit-and-debt/credit/tools/calculate-a-vehicle-payment?article_source=news_insights&article_category=education&article_name=buying-vs-leasing-your-first-car&article_cta=vehicle-payment-calculator) without building ownership in the vehicle.


Buying your first car is a major milestone, and one of the biggest financial decisions you'll make as a young adult. It’s an exciting step, but before you start comparing makes, models and features, you need to answer an important question: Should you buy used, buy new or lease?


Each option comes with different costs and tradeoffs. A used car may cost less upfront but require more maintenance, while a new car may offer greater reliability but at a higher price. Leasing can mean lower monthly payments and the flexibility to drive a newer vehicle, but you won’t own the car when the lease ends.


That’s why it’s important to look beyond the sticker price. Understanding what each option could cost now and over time can help you choose a car that meets your needs without stretching your budget.


## What are the benefits and drawbacks of leasing?


Leasing a car can be an appealing option if you want to drive a newer vehicle without buying it. Instead of paying toward ownership, your monthly payments generally cover the vehicle’s expected depreciation during the lease term, along with financing charges and fees. Since you're not financing the full purchase price, lease payments are often lower than loan payments for the same vehicle.


Most leases last a few years, after which you typically return the vehicle to the dealership or have the option to buy it. This works well if you like driving a new car every few years or want a vehicle that remains under warranty for most or all of the time you have it.


However, lower monthly payments don’t necessarily mean leasing is the cheaper option overall. Leases typically come with annual mileage limits, and exceeding them can result in additional charges. You may also be responsible for excess wear and tear, and ending a lease early can be costly.


The biggest tradeoff is ownership. When you finance a car, your payments eventually end and you’re left with a vehicle you own. With a lease, you generally return the car at the end of the term without an asset to sell or trade in. If your goal is to keep your first car for many years, buying may offer better long-term value.


## What are the benefits and drawbacks of buying used?


Buying used can be an attractive option for first-time car buyers looking to keep costs down. Used cars generally cost less than new ones, which can mean a smaller down payment, lower monthly payments and less money borrowed.


Buying used may also help you avoid some of the steepest depreciation. New cars typically lose value fastest in their first few years, so buying used means you’re paying less for a vehicle that still has plenty of life left.


The tradeoff is that an older car may come with less predictable expenses. Depending on its age, mileage and maintenance history, you might face repair or maintenance costs sooner than you would with a new car. Some used vehicles may also have limited warranty coverage or none at all.


Before buying used, consider more than just the price. A little research before you commit can help you understand the vehicle’s condition, anticipate future expenses and avoid costly surprises. Here are a few steps to take:


- **Check the vehicle history.** A vehicle history report can provide information about previous accidents, owners, title status and other details that could affect the car’s condition or value.
- **Get a pre-purchase inspection.** Consider having an independent, trusted mechanic inspect the vehicle before you buy. They can spot problems that aren’t obvious during a test drive.
- **Take a thorough test drive.** Try driving the car in different conditions, and pay attention to how it accelerates, brakes, steers and handles. Listen for unusual noises and test features such as the air conditioning, lights and electronics.
- **Research the model.** Look into the car's reliability, common problems and typical maintenance costs. Two used cars with similar prices and mileage can have very different long-term ownership costs.
- **Check insurance costs.** Insurance costs can vary considerably between cars, so getting a quote before making a purchase can give you a more accurate picture of what the car will cost each month.


A used car can offer significant savings, but the lowest price doesn’t always mean the lowest cost.


## What are the benefits and drawbacks of buying new?


Buying new typically costs more than buying used, but that higher price can come with greater predictability. You know the car's history from day one, and new cars generally require fewer major repairs in their first few years.


New vehicles also typically come with manufacturer warranties that cover certain repairs for a set period or mileage. That coverage can make unexpected repair bills less likely while the warranty is in effect, although you’ll still need to budget for routine expenses such as oil changes and new tires.


The biggest drawback is cost. Along with a higher purchase price, financing a new car may mean borrowing more and taking on a larger monthly payment. New vehicles also tend to depreciate fastest during their first few years, meaning the car can lose a significant portion of its value relatively early in your ownership.


Buying new may make sense if you have room in your budget for a higher purchase price and value the predictability of a brand-new car with warranty coverage. Just make sure that if you're financing it, the monthly payment fits comfortably alongside insurance, maintenance and your other financial priorities.


## Know your numbers before you shop


There’s no single right way to get your first car. Buying used may help you save upfront, buying new can offer more predictability and leasing may provide lower monthly payments and greater flexibility. The best choice is the one that fits your budget, driving needs and long-term plans.


Before you start shopping, look beyond the sticker price and consider the full cost of having a car, including your monthly payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance and other expenses.
